en: To deliberately hold back from doing or enjoying something; to not vote
hook: ABS-TAIN: to keep your ABS, you abstain from sweets.
story: During exam month, Nadia abstained from social media completely. She deleted the apps, gave her phone to her mother, and checked it only on Fridays. To abstain is to choose not to do something you might enjoy. In voting, to abstain means not voting yes or no; in the meeting, three members abstained.

en: Official approval or praise
hook: APPROBATION = APPROVAL (they look alike).
story: When the young scientist presented her flood-warning system, the senior professors nodded and applauded. Their approbation meant more to her than any prize; it showed that experts approved of her work. Approbation means approval or praise, often formal. Its opposite is opprobrium, which means public disgrace and harsh criticism.

en: To hold something dear; to protect and care for lovingly
hook: CHERISH: like a CHERRY on top, the most treasured part.
story: Rafi keeps an old, cracked watch that belonged to his late grandfather. It doesn't work anymore, but he cherishes it more than anything he owns. He keeps it wrapped in cloth and touches it before every exam. To cherish is to love and protect something deeply, like memories, people, or values.

en: To confirm or support with additional evidence
bn: সমর্থন করা; প্রমাণ দিয়ে নিশ্চিত করা
hook: CO-ROBORATE: CO-ROBUST, makes a claim stronger with a partner's evidence.
story: The shopkeeper said a man in a red cap stole the money. Police doubted him until the CCTV footage corroborated his story: there was the man, red cap and all, grabbing the cash. To corroborate is to support a claim with more evidence. In GRE science passages, new data often corroborate a hypothesis.

en: Fundamentally different; not able to be compared
hook: DISPARATE: DIS + PARITY. No parity, no equality; completely different.
story: The study group was made of disparate people: a shy engineer, a loud doctor, a quiet artist, and a businessman. They had nothing in common, yet they all wanted to study abroad. Disparate means very different in kind. Don't confuse it with desperate. Disparate things are so unlike that they can barely be compared.

en: To imitate someone you admire in order to match or surpass them
hook: EMULATE: your hero's EMblem; you copy them to become as good.
story: Young Shakib practiced every evening, trying to emulate his cricket hero: same stance, same bat grip, same calm focus. He didn't just copy; he wanted to become just as great, or even greater. To emulate is to imitate someone you admire, aiming to equal or beat them. Computer emulators imitate other systems.

en: To drain someone of energy or strength; to weaken
hook: TRAP: ENERVATE looks like ENERGIZE but means the opposite: it takes the NERVE out.
story: After nine hours in the stifling summer heat with no electricity, everyone in the house felt enervated, too tired even to talk. The heat had drained every drop of energy. Enervate means to weaken or exhaust. It's a classic GRE trap: it sounds like energize, but it means the exact opposite.

en: Lasting for a very short time
hook: EPHEMERAL: like an Instagram story, gone in a day.
story: Mitu's viral video got two million views in one day. She felt famous. A week later, nobody remembered it. Internet fame is ephemeral: bright, exciting, and gone almost instantly. Ephemeral means short-lived. Mayflies, soap bubbles, and trends are ephemeral; mountains and real friendships are not.

en: Intensely enthusiastic or passionate, sometimes excessively
hook: FERVID = FERVOR = FEVER of passion.
story: The fans outside the stadium were fervid, painting their faces green and red, chanting for hours, and crying with joy when Bangladesh won. Their passion was burning hot. Fervid means intensely enthusiastic, almost feverish. A fervid supporter of a cause will argue for it day and night.

en: Excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters
hook: GARRULOUS: sounds like GARGLE-ous, words gargling out nonstop.
story: The garrulous man on the train told Sara his entire life story in two hours: his childhood, his marriage, his diabetes, and his opinions on every cricketer. She just wanted to read her book. Garrulous means talking too much about unimportant things. It's a synonym of loquacious, but slightly more annoying.

en: Designed to start fires; tending to stir up conflict or anger
hook: INCENDIARY: think INCENSE that's lit, or a fire that's lit.
story: Police found incendiary devices, small bombs designed to start fires, hidden near the market. Weeks later, a politician gave an incendiary speech that inflamed crowds and sparked riots. Incendiary means fire-causing, either literally or figuratively. Incendiary words set people's anger on fire.

en: Harmful or hostile; tending to obstruct
hook: INIMICAL: contains 'enemy' (inimicus in Latin).
story: Late-night phone scrolling is inimical to good sleep, and poor sleep is inimical to learning. Tanvir learned this the hard way when he forgot half his vocab words. Inimical means harmful or unfriendly, acting like an enemy. A climate inimical to plant life is one where nothing can grow.

en: To suggest or hint indirectly
hook: GRE trick: as a verb, INTIMATE means to hint, like whispering an intimate secret.
story: The manager never said directly that Arif would be promoted. But she intimated it: 'You may want to start thinking about how you'd lead a team.' Arif understood the hint perfectly. As a verb, intimate means to suggest indirectly. As an adjective, intimate means close and personal, as in an intimate friendship.

en: To give strength, energy, and liveliness to
hook: IN-VIGOR-ate: puts VIGOR into you.
story: After four hours of studying, Nadia felt sleepy and dull. A quick walk in the cool evening air and a cup of strong tea invigorated her, and she studied for two more hours with fresh energy. To invigorate is to fill with life and energy. It's the opposite of enervate.

en: To make something less severe, serious, or painful
hook: MITIGATE: put MITTENS on the GATE — softens the blow.
story: Bangladesh cannot stop cyclones, but it has learned to mitigate their damage: early warnings, cyclone shelters, and evacuation drills have saved thousands of lives. To mitigate is to reduce the severity of something bad. Mitigating circumstances, like self-defense, make a crime seem less serious.

en: No longer in use; out of date
hook: OBSOLETE: 'OBviously SOLD long ago', not sold anymore.
story: Rafi found his father's old floppy disks in a drawer. He couldn't open them; no computer at home even had a floppy drive. The technology had become obsolete. Obsolete means no longer used or produced because something better has replaced it. Typewriters, pagers, and VCRs are obsolete.

en: Not transparent; hard to understand
hook: OPAQUE: light can't pass through; meaning can't pass through either.
story: The bathroom window was made of opaque glass, so light came in, but nobody could see through. Similarly, the professor's lecture was opaque; students couldn't see what he meant. Opaque means you can't see through something, either physically or intellectually. Its opposite is transparent, or lucid.

en: Serving as a typical or perfect example of something
hook: PARADIGM = a model. PARADIGMATIC = the model example.
story: When teachers explain a successful startup, they often use bKash as a paradigmatic case: a simple idea, a huge unmet need, and rapid growth. It's the textbook example. Paradigmatic means serving as a perfect model or typical example of a type. Paradigmatic is a fancy synonym of quintessential.

en: Overly concerned with minor details or rules; showing off learning
bn: পাণ্ডিত্য জাহির করে এমন; খুঁটিনাটি নিয়ে অতিরিক্ত মাথাব্যথা
hook: PEDANTIC: a PEDAL-pushing professor who corrects every tiny thing.
story: When Mitu said, 'Can I ask a question?', her pedantic cousin replied, 'You can; the question is whether you may.' He corrected grammar at dinner, quoted facts no one asked for, and fixed tiny errors in birthday cards. Pedantic means annoyingly fussy about small details and rules.

en: Calm and peaceful; not easily upset
hook: PLACID: a PLACE that's calm, like a still lake.
story: Early in the morning, the lake at Ramsagar was placid: not a ripple, just a smooth mirror reflecting the trees. Sara's grandmother had the same nature; even when the house was in chaos, she stayed calm and gentle. Placid means calm and undisturbed. Placid water, a placid temper, a placid face.

en: Strongly critical or controversial in argument
hook: POLEMICAL: POLE-vaulting into a fight; aggressive argument.
story: The columnist's polemical article attacked the education system so fiercely that hundreds of angry responses poured in within hours. Some loved it, others demanded an apology. Polemical writing is combative, designed to argue forcefully and provoke debate. A polemic is a strong verbal attack on a belief or policy.

en: Done suddenly without careful thought (adj.); to cause something to happen suddenly (verb)
hook: PRECIPITATE: like rain falling suddenly from the sky (precipitation).
story: Angry after one bad day, Tanvir made a precipitate decision: he quit his job without another offer in hand. Two months of unemployment taught him to think first. As an adjective, precipitate means hasty and rash. As a verb, it means to cause suddenly: the scandal precipitated the minister's resignation.

en: Great depth of insight, knowledge, or feeling
hook: PROFUNDITY = PROFOUND-ity.
story: Rabindranath Tagore wrote simple songs about rain and rivers, yet each line holds surprising profundity about love, loss, and life. Readers find new depth in them every time. Profundity means deep insight or intellectual depth. Its opposite is superficiality, or shallowness.

en: Accurately predicting what will happen in the future
hook: PROPHETIC: like a PROPHET who foretells the future.
story: Years ago, Nadia's grandfather warned, 'One day, everyone will carry a telephone in their pocket and forget how to talk face to face.' His words were prophetic; today, they describe every family dinner. Prophetic means accurately foretelling the future. A prophetic novel predicts events decades before they happen.

en: Acting with care and thought for the future; wise and careful
hook: PRUDENT: a PRUDE about risk; careful, never wild.
story: Instead of spending her first salary on a new phone, Sara saved half of it for emergencies. When her father fell ill months later, that money paid the hospital bills. Her prudent choice saved the family. Prudent means wise, careful, and sensible about the future. The opposite is imprudent, or rash.

en: Showing great attention to details or correct behavior
hook: PUNCTILIOUS: PUNCTUAL to the point; every point exactly right.
story: Mr. Rahman, the bank manager, was punctilious. He arrived at nine o'clock exactly, wore an ironed shirt every day, double-checked every figure, and answered every letter within a day. Punctilious means extremely careful about details and proper conduct. It's similar to meticulous, but with an emphasis on correct behavior.

en: Little known; obscure and hard to understand
hook: RECONDITE: RE-CON-DITE, hidden like a secret condo deep in the hills.
story: The professor's lecture on ancient Sanskrit grammar was so recondite that only two students in the hall understood it, and one of them was his own assistant. Recondite means obscure and difficult, known only to specialists. It's a synonym of arcane and abstruse, all heavy GRE words for hard-to-understand knowledge.

en: Very careful to do what is right; extremely attentive to detail
hook: SCRUPULOUS: has SCRUPLES, a moral conscience.
story: When the cashier accidentally gave Arif five hundred taka extra, he walked back three blocks to return it. He is scrupulous, careful to always do the right thing. Scrupulous means morally principled, and also extremely careful about details, as in scrupulous research. The opposite is unscrupulous: dishonest and without morals.

en: Free from disturbance; calm and peaceful
hook: TRANQUIL: like a TRANQUILIZER — calm.
story: After a noisy week in the city, Mitu spent a weekend at a tea garden in Sreemangal. Morning mist, birdsong, and endless green hills: everything was tranquil. For the first time in months, her mind was quiet. Tranquil means peacefully calm. Tranquilizer medicines are named after this feeling.

en: To keep changing one's mind; to waver between choices
hook: VACILLATE: OSCILLATE like a fan, swinging back and forth.
story: Should he apply to universities in the USA or Canada? Rafi vacillated for months: Canada on Monday, the USA on Tuesday, back to Canada on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the deadlines passed. To vacillate is to swing back and forth between opinions, unable to decide.
